The Short Britthers have performed a remarkable feat. They only entered for the transalantic flight a fortnight age, but are already making trial trips with the machine which they have assembled since signing the agreement. The Imperial Airways liner D.H. 34 had just left Croydon on Wednesday (Dec.24) when it nose dived after nearly striking a house on Purley Downs, and fell "like a stone". The petrol tanks burst and the machine was wrapped in flames. Seven passengers and the pilot were killed.

UNION OF WHISKY FIRMS.

Reasons for the fusion of the two Scotch whisky firms, Messrs. James Buchanan and Co., Ltd., and Messrs. John Dewar and Sons, Ltd., were given in an interview yesterday by Sir Thomas Dewar, the managing director of the latter firm:—

"By joining our forces," he said, "we shall be better able to take advantage of the large channels for the distribution of our goods, and we shall be able to co-operate in many ways to reduce expenses and lessen competition.

"It is a financial amalgamation only to enable us better to meet high taxes and the high price of raw material. The policy of the firms and with the conditions under which they work will be unchanged."
"Stamp fees alone in connection with the registration of the company will amount to nearly $40,000."

YOUNG FRENCH GENERALS
Young generals have taken the place of old in the French Army.
In the French official review, communicated by Reuter, it is stated that the higher command has been rejuvenated by the promotion of younger commanders of proved quality to high rank.

All the old generals who, at the beginning of August, were at the head of large commands have been gradually eliminated, some as the result of the physical strain of war, others by appointment to Territorial commands.

LONDON-PARIS PLANE IN FLAMES.

The Imperial Airways liner D.H. 34 had just left Croydon on Wednesday (Dec.24) when it nose dived after nearly striking a house on Purley Downs, and fell "like a stone". The petrol tanks burst and the machine was wrapped in flames. Seven passengers and the pilot were killed. Photo shows.. All that was left of the machine after the fire.

THE MYSTERY OF MR. HAMEL, THE AIRMAN: CHANNEL
SCOURED BY WARSHIPS AND AEROPLANES.
His only serious smash. His machine was wrecked in the Gordon-Bennett race of 1911.

Aeroplanes and warships scoured the Channel yesterday for Mr. Gustav Hamel, the famous airman, who has announced his intention of trying to fly across the Atlantic. He is stated to have started to fly from Boulogne to Hendon for the Aerial Derby, and the absence of any news of him is causing some anxiety, as the weather in the Channel was extremely bad for flying.-(Daily Mirror photographs.)

PILOTS GIVE AN AEROPLANE PICNIC.
Mr. Alcock and passenger.

Messrs. Edwin L. Gower and James Alcock have just given an aeroplane picnic, which is quite a new way of entertaining one's friends. A start was made from Brooklands, the guests flying with their hosts to the place appointed for tea. The idea was most successful, and a very jolly afternoon was spent.

INSIGNIA OF UNITED STATES FLYING SQUADRONS.

American aeroplanes over the Europe n battlefront will be distinguished by a white star with a red center on a circular field of blue. Aeroplanes will bear the star on the wings of the machine while it will be on the top and bottom of the gas bag of each dirigible. The rudders of the aeros will bear a distinguishing emblem. They will be painted with stripes of red, white, and blue.

Secretary of the Navy Daniels has issued a general order for all naval aircraft to adopt the insignia. This emblem has been the insignia identified with the Layfayette Escadrille, the American flying squad- ron with the French army. Enel of the principal reasons that influenced the adoption of this particular figure is that it has been so successfully and XIVically worn by American airmen who have made for themselves and their country a reputation as daring, capable fighting aviators while flying for France.
Each of the fighting nations have some distinctive mark painted in some prominent spot on their aeroplanes by which their aircraft are easily recognized.

NEWS ITEM--This machine is a Handley Page for Rolls Royce 350 horse power engine known as The Berlin Barber, which has just arrived at Newfoundland and is to a Attempt the Trans Atlantic flight some wine during the month of June. Fully loaded it weighs 15 tons. Over five tons of which is useful load. The wing span is 126 feet the width of the span is 12 feet and the length of the fuselage is 65 feet.

One of these machines flew from Ipswich, England to India a distance of 5800 miles last winter and covered 700 miles of the trip over the Mediterranean which was a record flight for a land machine flying over water.

This type of machine will be used to a very large extent in Commercial aviation being able to carry a five ton load up of people, mail or merchandise in a non-top flight between Boston and St.Louis within twelve hours.

The latest addition to scientific invention and development is the flying motor car, recently exhibited in a successful demonstration. The new machine, an invention of M. Campier, a Frenchman can either fly or travel by road as required. The machine has the appearance of a biplane when flying and when used as a motor car the wings are folded back to the side of the body. For land travel it has two engines but on ordinary speed only one need be used, that of ten horsepower, while for air travel, the other engine of three hundred horse power is necessary. It's trial was given recently at Buc, Seine-et-Oise and all the usual feats of an automobile and and aeroplane were performed. Photo shows the two different appearances. The upper half shows the machine as an automobile, the wings being folded back, and the lower half, as an aeroplane.
